title.narrative: HortIMPACT

description.narrative:
At company and beneficiaries level (mostly farmers), business cases play a pivotal role in introducing and demonstrating best horticultural practices and applicable solutions. Business Cases (BC), including their supply chain context, are the ultimate proof that innovative and appropriate technologies, business models or solutions, that are already used and proven to be beneficial elsewhere, also are effective under Kenyan conditions and are commercially viable and beneficial for the horticultural sector.
BCs are the core of the HortIMPACT approach and are instrumental to achieving the results under objective 1. By facilitating BCs, medium and small sized farmers and their organisations will be directly connected to markets or through lead firms or trader associations. Without exception HortIMPACT BCs need to be sustainable and commercially successful. The BCs need to address and be supportive to one, two or all of the three thematic programme issues. Solutions developed in HortIMPACT BCs should have the potential for adoption by large numbers of medium and smallholders in due course. A scaling strategy for HortIMPACT was developed, however not fully implemented, as concluded by the MTR. Also the MTR recommended to make a stronger link between the BCs and objective 2 related to systemic changes at sector level.
To respond to the recommendations in the MTR, the scaling-up of business cases will be analyzed and addressed in an earlier stage with the use of concrete tools, such as the Adopt, Adapt, Expand and Respond framework and the PPPLab scaling scan tool. Scaling up will be looked into at the level of systemic change in the sector/value chain, through addressing supporting services and/or the regulatory framework (mostly through public sector involvement). Solutions or best practices, developed in the various BCs will be disseminated through working at these levels. The purpose is to engage sector and industry organisations in advancing the sector.
HortIMPACT is pursuing a Public Private Partnership approach to address those issues that are in the interest of the horticultural sector - companies as well as the Government of Kenya and society. To successfully address the three critical HortIMPACT issues, a joint public private agenda and interventions are the key for targeted success.

Goal: To contribute to increased food security and increased incomes through the development of a dynamic and sustainable horticulture sector in Kenya inclusive of small and medium sized farmers.
Objectives: 1. Entrepreneurial capacities and performance of small and medium sized Kenyan farmers and companies enhanced for improved market access to domestic and international markets.
2. Systemic challenges related to inclusion of small and medium sized farmers in market oriented supply chains, food safety issues and reducing food losses in the horticulture sector effectively addressed.

HortIMPACT builds on the lessons learnt and scales up the experiences of the ‘Horticulture and Food Security Programme' (HFSP) that was executed from 2012 until 2014. HortIMPACT complies with and supports the objectives of the Multi Annual Strategic Plan of the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Kenya, in particular the food security and aid to trade agenda. HortIMPACT is also aligned with the agricultural strategy and policies of the Government of Kenya. The programme closely cooperates with Dutch and Kenyan entrepreneurs and makes use of their advanced technologies, products and market linkages in so-called business cases. The focus of the programme is on small and medium sized entrepreneurial farmers and farming as a ‘family unit’. Simultaneously HortIMPACT addresses policy and market related, systemic issues at service provision, industry/value chain and government level, supported by results from the innovative and market oriented business cases.
HortIMPACT contributes to increased food security, increased incomes and a dynamic and sustainable horticulture sector in Kenya. Three themes, crucial for further development of the horticulture sector are being addressed by the programme: 1) inclusion of small and medium sized entrepreneurial farmers in supply chains; 2) improving food safety and integrated crop protection and 3) reducing food losses and efficiency in supply chains. HortIMPACT mostly focuses on fruits and vegetables.

HortIMPACT kicks off in January 2015 with 3 months inception phase. During this phase, preparations for actual implementation will be made. Interviews will be carried out , preferred service providers will be identified, baseline studies, and finalisation of the programme's operational framework will be concluded.
By end of inception phase the HortIMPACT team will have concretized the demands of the companies, County Governments, National Agencies, Associations and other parties. A kick-off workshop and launch of the HortIMPACT will mark the end of this phase.

KMHP works with the following target groups:
* Organised small and medium sized entrepreneurial farmers and their organisations. * International (Dutch) and Kenyan agricultural companies, including processors, traders, brokers, exporters, importers, retailers, input suppliers and their organisations, as well as, other support service providers such as financing institutions. * Government of Kenya organisations and institutions, training institutes and industry and consumers’ organisations.

The HortIMPACT program does also address systemic challenges in order to further leverage the potential of the Kenyan horticulture sector and to capture market opportunities benefiting more small and medium sized farmers. Thus, the sustainability of the HortIMPACT programme is ensured by addressing the identified three systemic issues (farmers inclusion, food safety and food losses), through a coordinated effort at the three required levels (i)SMEs / farms, (ii) support services and industry organisations, and (iii) Government. After each Business Case is concluded, an evaluation and reassessed scaling strategy is developed to carry the impacts and lessons learned sustainably further.
This mechanism will provide opportunities for large number of horticultural producers to participate in market oriented value chains in the mid and long term and thus contribute to increased food security and income generation. Furthermore this upscaling process from farm/ company level to sector level will contribute to a dynamic horticulture sector with sustained growth, higher incomes, more employment and improved food security in Kenya.

The unique Kenya Market-led Horticulture Programme (HortIMPACT) approach entails cooperation with Dutch and Kenyan agricultural entrepreneurs, both small and medium sized farmers, input providers, exporters and traders in so called business cases. Business cases will benefit from advanced but appropriate technologies and products, improved agricultural practices and market linkages.

Yielder (K) Limited proposes to develop Yielder, a platform to improve the communication between farmers and knowledge centers and vice versa. The goal of many NGOs and knowledge centers is to create bigger food safety and food security by improving farming. Reaching out to farmers seems difficult and comes with a high cost. Only a small percentage is actually reached effectively. The explosive spread of (smart) phones makes it possible to share information with farmers at a low cost and the information comes in an easy accessible way. The Yielder platform is a bridge between the knowledge centers and the farmers; farmers can ask questions to their colleagues and knowledge centers. And knowledge centers can push relevant information to farmers.

06-12-2019: The Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Fisheries (MOALF) organised a multi-stakeholder workshop in Nairobi to roll out interventions that address food safety for the horticulture subsector through the National Horticulture Transformation Technical Working Group (NHTTWG) in lilne with the ongoing processes of developing legal framework for a National Food Safety Agency by the National Government in recognition of the importance of food safety in the national development agenda. The objective of the workshops was to examine and scale up interventions supporting improved food safety for increased competitiveness of the horticulture sub-sector with a focus on traceability of fresh produce for domestic markets. the dialogue was expected to bring an element of responsibility were: 1. Government agencies will proactively and neutrally implement the various food safety control system measures 2. County governments will support producer organisations and market transfers with necessary technical and infrastructure support 3. Private sector value chain actors will proactively implement GAP, GMP, and HACCP and undertake self-regulation 4. Consumers will actively demand assurance of safety of their food from food business operators. The outcome of the workshop was that KEPSA will table food safety motion bill with the Senate which will potentially become a law. The rationale behind including the central government convened workshop in this indicator is/was that, deliberations and action plans made in this forum will directly have an impact on county governments’ implementation of food safety regulations.

After the exchange visit, Mwea and Limuru farmers came back and adopted some of the GAP practices learnt in Tanzania example Mwea farmer group started a seed raising business and adopted soil sterilizing techniques they learnt from a seed raiser in Tanzania. After their first attempt to seed raise, the group got 70-74% germination rate which is accepted when you’re plant raising for the first time. 6 farmer groups from BC11 visited Instaveg pack house to learn and witness quality seedling raising in the nursery and market quality requirements in the packhouse as part of food safety regulations.

title.narrative: Impact: To contribute to increased food security and increased incomes through the development of a dynamic and sustainable horticulture sector in Kenya with inclusion of small and medium-sized farmers.

comment.narrative: 05-12-2019: BC15 132 farmers were trained on food safety (33 of whom were GAP certified), contracted and supplied safe food to Instaveg who in turn supplied the first traceable produce to supermarkets like Eastmatt, BC11 126 farmers were contracted and supplied potatoes to Sereni fries therefore got stable prices for their potatoes as a result of the contract, BC9 6000 farmers are now using the cold storage installed by Meru Greens and the result is there has been a 12% reduction of rejects, BC1 Scale up 218 farmers were contracted and are supplying safely produced vegetables to Neighbourhood Freshmart having been trained on use of biologicals and so far 93 farmers are buying Koppert products like traps.

10-01-2018: Results that have come in so far from our ongoing impact evaluation of business case 1 point to a growing number of farmers who have adopted among other techniques Integrated pest management. As a result of IPM adoption, 24% of farmers in BC1 have reported less prevalence of pests and diseases which can be attributed to the use of IPM methods therefore enhancing production of safe food.

13-03-2019: After doing our assessment with BC6 Ithanga farmers, Ketchup innovation Kwakyai farmers and BC2 endline one mango growing farmer discussed in detail how he embraced IPM after GAP training to produce safe mangoes and how IPM has enabled him reduce loss of mangoes to pests and diseases. "In the recent past (before GAP training), after I pruned my mangoes, I thought the leaves and all the fruits falling were manure. This is the kind of thinking I had. After pruning I would leave the leaves lying the ground. After training (GAP), I came to learn that when the fruits fall, the reasons for their fall are pests and the pests are still in the fruit multiplying. The leaves too had diseases and after pruning, they are still infected. I have learnt that farm hygiene for mangoes and oranges reduces diseases because if you do it the right way and when you spray the right way you will eliminate pests drastically. When we compare how we’re doing farming now and how we did farming before, I can say there has been a lot of changes and differences between farms of GAP certified farmers and our neighbours (not GAP certified) such that during harvesting, a lot of our neighbours mangoes fall down and they can see our mangoes are not falling down. Some of our neighbours have even asked us why we border each other yet their mangoes have not multiplied and ours have multiplied. I told my neighbour about farm hygiene, told him to look at his farm and my farm and notice that he did not prune well so there is no good circulation of air. I asked him how he sprays and he said during flowering so I told him you’re supposed to start spraying after pruning and not when mangoes start flowering. If you fail in farm hygiene, spraying after pruning, you have failed in farming. Our neighbours have seen us buying traps and are also buying traps as a way of mitigating the challenge that surrounds us (pests)."

21-03-2018: No endline for business cases was done in 2017. However it is worth noting that, Makueni cooperative was awarded a tender by Makueni County government to supply mangoes to the newly commissioned fruit processing plant in Makueni. 50 tomato farmers in Kwakyai Rural SACCO have been trained and 35 GAP certified on tomato production and are supplying dried tomatoes to The Ketchup Company. 22 farmers who are also GAP certified are delivering mangoes to Bamber & Burton.

06-12-2019: Farmers from Meru Greens (BC9, 3500 farmers) are now using two cold storage facilities installed in Meru and Nandi. Sereni fries farmers (BC11, 474 farmers) were trained on good practices that produce potatoes meant for the cold store. These potatoes need to be produced with certain specifications. The cold store has been installed at the farm level in Nakuru and is accessible to all Sereni Fries trained potato farmers. Instaveg business case (BC15) had 214 farmers trained on GAP and 33 were certified. 6 collection centres for Instaveg have been set up and one refrigerated Truck for product deliveries was bought so that trained farmers can easily aggregate their produce.

10-01-2018: Makueni fruit tree innovation trained farmers in Makueni, Narok, Bomet and Kericho counties. Farmers were introduced to the use of pheromone traps to control fruit fly. Fruit fly has been a menace in mangoes and led to a lot of waste after harvesting.
There was a 3535 deficit in 2016 which was carried forward to 2017

21-03-2018: BC6 has trained 1022 farmers on GAP and 22 have been GAP certified. Part of GAP training was controlling fruit flies which has been a major contributor to loss of mangoes. 22 farmers who are GAP certified and supplying mangoes to B&B are using fruit fly traps to control fruit flies. GAP training also involves how to identify the right fruit to pick to prevent picking unripe mangoes that will go into waste. Under the Ketchup project, 50 farmers were trained on good agricultural practices and 36 were GAP certified. The GAP certified and are now supplying dried tomatoes in the Netherlands. Drying of tomatoes is being done using a solar drier. The bulk of the farmers will be linked to cold storage facilities in 2018 under BC9.
